book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

chapters.file: ch84 - The Myth of the ‘Well-Informed’ Citizen.md
chapters.relation: Mark Evans opens the book's political section by insisting that politicians mostly produce bullshit rather than lies in Frankfurt's strict sense: lying requires knowing and concealing the truth, while the Bush administration's WMD case for invading Iraq shows truth-indifference, with post-hoc 'rejustifications' (humanitarian intervention, democratisation, Saddam-9/11 hints) spun as needed. Using G.A. Cohen's distinction between aim-bullshitters and disposition-bullshitters, it reads Winston Smith's routinized rewriting of The Times in Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four as falsehood that slides from lying into bullshit, since the Party aims to destroy the very true/false distinction. Totalitarian regimes (Havel's 'living in truth') thus embed themselves not in a web of lies but in a morass of bullshit insulated from any possibly refuting facts.

chapters.file: ch85 - ‘Dumbing-Up’ Some Distortions of Democratic Equality.md
chapters.relation: Evans argues that democratic citizens do their own share of Frankfurt-bullshitting about politics: because electoral democracy cannot admit how complex politics really is, it institutionalizes the fictional ideal of the 'well-informed' citizen, obliging voters to hold over-simplified views and politicians to pander to them. Campaigning forces candidates into dodges like the 'politics of distraction' and the empty promise to be 'a different sort of politician', producing 'Governor Schwarzenegger Syndrome' and opening space for dangerous demagogues and fundamentalisms. Following Churchill, the chapter concludes that this citizen-side bullshit vindicates the cynicism thesis only partially and gives no reason to reject democracy as 'the worst form of government except for all the others'.

The chapter claims that 'equal respect' in modern democracies has been distorted into a 'dumbing-up' relativism — 'I'm valid, you're valid' — which conflates the equal right to voice opinions with their equal intellectual merit and so leaves nothing that counts as bullshit. It illustrates this through the 'democratization of expertise' and management-speak ('downsizing', 'mission statements'), which mimics profundity while evading awkward facts, and it tests and rejects the quasi-Nietzschean ressentiment story of timid citizens dragging discourse down to a common denominator. To get the full measure of the phenomenon it expands Frankfurt's and Cohen's typologies into seven kinds of bullshit, adding clarifiable unclarity, plain rubbish, irretrievable speculation, pretension, and evasion.

chapters.file: ch87 - Chapter 13 - Political Bullshit and the Stoic Story of Self.md
chapters.relation: Evans concludes that the antidote to political bullshit is a discursive culture trained in Socratic skills of self-examination — citizens taught to recognize how their own views may be imperfect and how to refine them — together with the analytic-philosophical style his Oxford tutor called 'a very good bullshit detector'. Experts may lead debates by their greater factual knowledge and critical acumen, but the debates must stay democratically inclusive rather than become an elite monopoly. Citing G.A. Cohen, he warns that too much fashionable philosophy disparages truth and so itself produces bullshit, and that using the ubiquity of bullshit to justify the cynicism thesis's crippling inertia would be potentially catastrophic.

Vanessa Neumann sets out a third strategy for analyzing bullshit, beside Frankfurt's agent-centered and G.A. Cohen's content-centered definitions: studying the mechanism of bullshit, the speaker-listener relation through which it works in political discourse. Bullshit need not be false — even true statements can be non-germane or obfuscatory — and it serves two purposes: depicting the speaker as desirable ('I'm one of you') and targeting groups ('they are different from us, so we should treat them like this'). Its key trick is moral language without moral commitment, as when a politician condemns a rival's corporate free trip without explaining why it is wrong, scoring points while preserving wiggle room for future favors of their own.

Building on Peter Goldie's account of how life-narratives shape emotion, and Martha Nussbaum's view of emotions as judgments of value and importance (which the chapter identifies with the Greek Stoic view), it explains where bullshit gets its power over us. Because an episode's place in a narrative determines what we feel — Oedipus could be delighted to have married Jocasta but not his mother — bullshit works by 'educating' our emotions, telling us what should make us proud, patriotic, angry or frightened, and what belongs in a eudaimonistic life. It closes by warning that bullshit appeals to the base and non-rational part of us and so degrades us, before turning to examples from international politics.

chapters.file: ch91 - Chapter 14 - Bullshit at the Interface of Science and Policy Global Warming,.md
chapters.relation: The chapter dissects 'we are waging a war on terror' word by word: the inclusive 'we' conscripts the listener, 'war' triggers unquestioning patriotism, and 'terror' — an emotion, rather than 'terrorists' or 'terrorism' — keeps the enemy suitably vague, a bogeyman Other to hunt. The phrase is bullshit not because fighting terrorism is wrong but because it replaces the thought and debate that democratic policy and military decisions require with fear management, and militant jihadists' 'God's will' rhetoric works the same way, never explaining how bombing or torturing the uninvolved will end fear. Both sides use bullshit to supply identity and purpose while evading genuine moral justification, which degrades our capacity to be moved by ideas.

chapters.file: ch92 - Bullshit of the Isolated Fact.md
chapters.relation: Heather Douglas opens her chapter on science advice by framing the problem with Plato's parable of the stargazer as expert navigator for the ship of state in the Republic, tracing the debate from excluding pseudoscience through 'junk science' to 'politicized science'. She identifies two kinds of bullshit at the science-policy interface: true-but-misleading statements that exploit technical complexity to confuse the public about uncertainty, and appeals to a nonexistent universal standard of 'sound science' that actually smuggle in judgments about the consequences of error. Remedies include constant vigilance and reframing debates around the explicit weighing of evidence, uncertainty, and the risks of getting things wrong.

The chapter explains 'bullshit of the isolated fact' through the climate-change debate: skeptics like Robert Balling and Fred Singer repeatedly cited the 1940-1975 cooling trend as incompatible with human-caused warming while omitting the aerosol research — confirmed when models correctly predicted the cooling after Mt. Pinatubo's 1991 eruption — which shows sulfate scrubbing had been masking the greenhouse signal. Likewise the satellite-versus-ground temperature discrepancy, which skeptics took as disproof, dissolved once instrument errors were re-examined. Repeating an isolated fact after its debunking has been publicized in Science or National Academy reports is, with Frankfurt, to reveal oneself unconcerned with the truth — willing to spread bullshit to win.

chapters.file: ch94 - Combatting the Two Kinds of Bullshit.md
chapters.relation: Douglas argues that 'universal standards bullshit' — the assumption that evidence must meet one threshold before it counts as scientific — comes from textbook schooling and has no warrant: there is no such standard, and we shouldn't want one. She shows how it distorts debate on all sides, from Bush administration uncertainty claims to Michael Gough's Popper-inspired insistence that climate models cannot be tested, and argues that whether evidence suffices always depends on the risks of error — the gas-gauge warning versus the bomb in your car. Genuine politicization (suppressing evidence, firing researchers) must be condemned, but deciding how much uncertainty is acceptable is an ineliminably political and ethical judgment.

chapters.file: ch95 - Chapter 15 - Rhetoric Is Not Bullshit.md
chapters.relation: Douglas concludes that the two kinds of bullshit need different remedies. Isolated-fact bullshit — Fred Singer's commentaries resting on selective omission and emphasis — can only be met with vigilance, since the public forum must remain open and even its spreaders may not grasp the nature of their claims. Universal-standards bullshit, by contrast, can be permanently undermined once we recognize there are no such standards: asking instead about the strength of evidence and the risks of error, and getting used to expert disagreement, would deflate the persuasive power of a single isolated fact.

chapters.file: ch96 - The Problem (and Politics) of Rhetoric.md
chapters.relation: David Tietge opens his defense of rhetoric with the aphorism that rhetoric isn't devious and untrustworthy — those are features reserved for language itself — and reports a semester-long count in which 156 of 157 media uses of 'rhetoric' were pejorative, the sole exception being George Carlin telling Jon Stewart that a comedian is essentially a rhetorician who unpacks how words mean. He traces rhetoric's decline from its honored place in the Trivium of the Seven Liberal Arts, notes the societal paradox that we condemn 'bullshit' yet richly reward lawyers, politicians, and advertising executives for producing it, and promises to dissolve the crude truth/falsity dichotomy that fuels the identification of rhetoric with bullshit.

The chapter distinguishes Aristotle's rhetorica utens — his On Rhetoric as a civic how-to primer — from rhetorica docens, the modern theoretical study of how language means, arguing that Aristotle's practical bias left the public unable to see rhetoric as a method of textual analysis. It then performs such an analysis on George W. Bush's statement on the Alito nomination ('bring dignity to the process... a fair hearing and an up-or-down vote'), showing how 'dignity' stigmatizes extended debate, 'fair hearing' is subjective, and the demand for decisiveness rails against contemplation — the reading The Onion satirized as 'Fair, Quick, Unanimous Confirmation'. Tietge defends his own admitted dislike of Bush as proof that declared subjectivity need not compromise a reading's integrity, since all language reflects personal and collective orientations.

Following Jeremy Campbell's The Liar's Tale, the chapter argues that the truth/lies binary is oversimplified: even 'the sky is blue' depends on contested definitions and 'God is good' on the speaker's concepts, so we must separate capital-T Truth — the immutable, incorruptible kind Plato located beyond the flawed physical realm of perfect Forms, which made him scorn rhetoric and the Sophists as teachers of disguise — from lower-case, situated, perspectival truths. It then recruits Nietzsche, for whom humans have no 'organ' for Truth but a natural instinct for falsehood (shared with camouflaging animals), and Ken Gemes's reading of doctrinal Truth as a ritualized fiction manufactured to maintain institutional and religious power. On this view postmodernism studies truth within the shifting domain of language rather than denying objective reality.

Tietge argues that postmodernism, far from denying objective reality, supplies a vocabulary for how language and interpretation shape small-t truths, and that rhetoric — Kenneth Burke's 'logology', words used to talk about words — is the discipline uniquely built to study this; hence rhetoric and bullshit are 'not even distant cousins'. He concedes Frankfurt's 'talk without knowing what he is talking about' catches genuine bullshit, like the student paper opener 'In today's society, there are many things that people have different and similar opinions about', and allows that 'salesman syndrome' rhetoric can be bullshit when its pitch is too transparent to persuade anyone. His remedy is to learn rhetoric — through hypothetical situations, deconstructing model essays, and keeping a commonplace book — since navigating the gray area between Truth and bullshit without understanding how language works leaves us to avoid the pitfalls by sheer chance.

chapters.file: ch100 - Bullshit as a Call to Open-Mindedness.md
chapters.relation: Steve Fuller opens by asking whether bullshit detection coarsens the detector: Nietzsche and H.L. Mencken embraced the debunker's role (Mencken coining 'bunk'), while Ibsen's The Wild Duck and Hedda Gabler dramatize the need for a 'life lie', and detectors who find bullshit everywhere slide from nihilism into dogmatism. He re-reads bullshit as sophistry — the Sophists taught that securing your audience's belief is the only knowledge you need, against Socrates's attack and Plato's coining of 'rhetoric' to demonize them — and faults Frankfurt for calling the bullshitter 'indifferent' to truth when the accomplished bullshitter must be a keen student of what people tend to regard as true. The Sokal affair and Benjamin Franklin's 'economical with the truth' lead to his Kantian mapping of bullshitters (rationalists selecting among already-imaginable alternatives) against bullshit detectors (empiricists demanding evidence), which the scientific method will dialectically synthesize.

chapters.file: ch101 - Wittgenstein Ultimate Bullshit Detector—or Bullshitter.md
chapters.relation: Fuller argues that mastering a discipline converts critics into loyal insiders — Thomas Kuhn's 'normal science' enshrines the tendency, cognitive dissonance explains it, and Blaise Pascal's wager is the general model of betting on a way of life that makes you receptive to its confirming signs. Against this he sets the Protestant tradition of Luther's conscience, 'playing it by ear', which like the Sophists concedes that reality rarely yields yes-or-no answers — the gap we fill being bullshit — and he frames the dispute as realism versus antirealism, reading Frankfurt's On Bullshit as an ad hominem attack on antirealists. He then re-examines Frankfurt's star witness: Wittgenstein's rebuke of Fania Pascal for saying she felt 'like a dog that has been run over' now looks like a spectacular lack of imagination, since evolutionary psychology, being forged at that very moment, has been narrowing the human-animal mental gap ever since.

chapters.file: ch102 - Bullshit as Deferred Epistemic Gratification.md
chapters.relation: The chapter reverses Frankfurt's verdict: Wittgenstein may himself have been a grandmaster of bullshit who practiced 'ventriloquism', speaking through the authority of ordinary language and 'paradigm case' examples, and whose scolding of Fania Pascal strikes some readers today like a priest fussing over a parishioner's impure thoughts. His bullshit was backward-looking ('you already know this'), unlike the forward-looking promissory bullshit of Galileo, whose deferred vindication Paul Feyerabend used to argue that the Papal Inquisitors were originally justified in their skepticism. Ernest Gellner's ostracized diagnosis — that Wittgenstein fed off British class anxiety most clearly marked in language use — is resisted both because careers ride on his authority and because his erratic 'idiot savant' persona keeps bullshit from sticking to him.

chapters.file: ch103 - The Scientific Method as a Search for the Justice in Bullshit.md
chapters.relation: Fuller portrays the bullshitter as the consummate hypocrite, bluffing from behind genuine uncertainty and exploiting the sophistic principle that controlling the moment of decision controls its outcome — calling the question when the balance of arguments favors you. Since we can rarely audit anyone's track record, epistemology leans on 'trust', 'witness' and 'testimony', read optimistically through Thomas Reid's divinely guaranteed common sense or, à la Kierkegaard, malignly as cowardly delegation of belief; either way 'reliability', which papers over the gap between evidence and belief, is itself a bullshit concept. He then analogizes the epistemic economy of evidence to the moral economy of sensation: as utilitarianism defers immediate gratification (taxation insuring against discounting our future selves), so the bullshitter's imperviousness to current evidence-weightings is prudence — an 'affirmative action' for weaker-evidenced positions that may prove the better bet in the fullness of time.

chapters.file: ch104 - Our Distinguished Panel of Incomparable Geniuses.md
chapters.relation: Fuller's finale casts Francis Bacon's scientific method as an inquisitorial trial designed to manage bullshit: everyone may produce it, provided a third-party judge frames a 'crucial experiment' that decides between the parties — a vision only partially realized by the Royal Society and later positivism, and tempered by Karl Popper's open-society point that all may bullshit to their heart's content given agreement on how to clean up after it. He tests the model on the Lomborg affair (initially found 'scientifically dishonest', then acquitted on appeal because politicized research is the environmental norm), on Zola's J'Accuse and Galileo's vindication in Newton's Principia as productive bullshit, and on his own service as expert witness: McLean v. Arkansas cut through creationist and evolutionist bullshit with a neutral definition of science, while Kitzmiller v. Dover adopted a 'methodological naturalism' custom-built to exclude Intelligent Design — justice losing out to the side whose bullshit is piled higher and deeper.

holes.name: G.A. Cohen
holes.what: Analytic socialist philosopher whose essay 'Deeper into Bullshit' defined bullshit as unclarifiable unclarity and distinguished aim-bullshitters from disposition-bullshitters.
holes.why: Chapter 84 deploys Cohen's aim/disposition-bullshitter distinction to classify political bullshit, and chapters 86, 87 and 89 build on his content-based typology as the book's second pillar beside Frankfurt.

holes.name: Peter Goldie
holes.what: Philosopher of emotion who argued that a person's life-narrative shapes and gives content to their emotional episodes and values.
holes.why: Chapter 90 builds its mechanism of political bullshit on Goldie's narrative theory of emotion, citing his work at nearly every step.

holes.name: Rhetoric (ethos, pathos, logos)
holes.what: The art of persuasive speech and the discipline that studies how language moves audiences, systematized by Aristotle in his Rhetoric.
holes.why: Chapter 96 (and book chapter 15, 'Rhetoric Is Not Bullshit', chapters 96-99) is devoted to defending rhetoric from identification with bullshit, and the taxonomy has no rhetoric entry at all.
